function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run inside a script).  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to create/modify.  

> ⚠️ **Important** – I’m assuming the repo contains a very small “Hello World” Node.js app that listens on port 3000.  
> If the real repo differs (different start‑up command, different port, etc.) simply adjust the values accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update `Dockerfile`

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json + package-lock.json first so we can cache dependencies
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> - `node:18-alpine` is a small, secure base image.  
> - `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> - `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical port for a Node “welcome” app.  
> - `CMD ["node", "index.js"]` runs the server.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML (`k8s.yaml`)

Create a file named `k8s.yaml` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                 # external port
    targetPort: 3000         # internal container port
```

> *What this does:*  
> - Deploys two replicas of the container.  
> - Exposes the app via a LoadBalancer (adjust as needed).  
> - Maps external port 80 → internal port 3000.

### 2.3 Create GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/build.yml`)

Create the following directory structure if it doesn’t exist:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

Then create a file named `.github/workflows/build.yml` with this content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Node.js App

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings**  
> - `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> - `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (create one under Settings → Security → Personal Access Tokens)  

> *What this workflow does:*  
> - Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> - Builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile above.  
> - Pushes the image to Docker Hub under the tag `latest`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, building and publishing the Docker image.  
If you’re using a different container registry (e.g., GitHub Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry), just adjust the `tags:` line in the workflow and the `image:` field in the Kubernetes YAML accordingly.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the workflow finishes, verify the image exists:

```bash
docker pull <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

And test the Kubernetes deployment locally (if you have `kubectl` configured):

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
kubectl get pods
kubectl get svc
```

That’s it! 🎉 If anything in the repo differs from my assumptions, tweak the values in the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, or workflow file accordingly.
